  • The most common relative pronouns are:

  • The past participle i.e. encouraged of the given verb has been used as the given sentence is in the past tense.
     

​​Correct Sentence: It was he who encouraged me when I was feeling low.

​​​​Additional Information  ​

  • ​​We use 'which' in relative clauses to refer to animals and things.
  • Example:
    • You need to tick the box which says yes.

questions.q:
Spot the error in the given sentence and select the correct sentence from the options given.

The award was given to the two employees, Mr. Sharma and myself.
o: The award was given to the two employees, Mr. Sharma and me.
The award was given to the two employees, Mr. Sharma and I.
The award was gave to the two employees, Mr. Sharma and myself.
The award was given for the two employees, Mr. Sharma and myself.
questions.s:
The error is the misuse of a reflexive pronoun.

Reflexive Pronouns: Reflexive pronouns (like myself, yourself, himself) are used when the subject and the object of the verb are the same person (e.g., "I hurt myself"). They cannot be used as a simple object of a verb or a preposition.

In the sentence, "myself" is used as the object of the preposition "to". This is incorrect. The correct pronoun to use as an object is "me". A simple way to check is to remove the other person: "The award was given to me" is correct, while "The award was given to myself" is incorrect.

Option a) is correct because it uses the correct objective pronoun "me" after the preposition "to".

Option b) is incorrect because "I" is a subjective pronoun and cannot be the object of the preposition "to".

Option c) is incorrect because the passive voice requires "was given" (was + v3), not "was gave" (was + v2), and it still uses the wrong pronoun.

Option d) is incorrect because it uses the wrong preposition ("for") and the wrong pronoun ("myself"). "Given to" is used when specifying the recipient of something.

Hence, option (a) is the correct answer.

Note: Reflexive Pronouns: Reflexive pronouns include myself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, and themselves. These are used to refer back to the subject of the clause in which they are used: She hurt herself in the eye.

Subjective Pronouns: The pronouns I, you, we, he, she, it, and they are known as subjective pronouns because they act as the subjects of verbs: We went to the party.

Objective Pronouns: The pronouns me, you, us, him, her, it, and them are called objective pronouns because they act as the objects of verbs and prepositions: Anjali drove us home.

V1 -> Base form/simple form of verb, V2 -> Past form of verb (-ed form or irregular verb), V3 -> Past participle form of verb (-ed, -d, -t, -en, or -n), V4 -> Continuous form of verb / Present participle form of verb (-ing form), V5 -> Third person singular (V1+ -es or -s).

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.

The police officer confirmed that it was ________ who reported the theft.
questions.s:
The context of the sentence is identifying the person who performed the action of reporting. The blank is part of a construction following the verb "to be" ("was") and renames the subject "it". In formal English, when a pronoun follows a form of the verb "to be" and renames the subject, it should be in the subjective case.

The correct option is "he". 'He' is the subjective pronoun and correctly functions as the predicate nominative, identifying who the subject 'it' was.

The other options do not fit: "him" is the objective case and is incorrect in this formal construction; "himself" is a reflexive pronoun; "his" is a possessive pronoun.

Thus, the complete sentence is: "The police officer confirmed that it was he who reported the theft."

Hence, option (a) is the correct answer.

Note:

Reflexive Pronouns: Reflexive pronouns include myself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, and themselves. These are used to refer back to the subject of the clause in which they are used: She hurt herself in the eye.

Possessive Pronouns: The pronouns mine, yours, hers, his, ours, and theirs are known as possessive pronouns: they refer to something owned by the speaker or by someone or something previously mentioned. For example: The pen is mine.
